IV10-01.note: Clean but thin. hopeful/curious/polite share no semantic field with WARY, so the item is decided by whether the student knows the word at all. 'curious' is the only one with any pull (both name a stance toward the unknown) and it is faint. Fine as an opener; carries no diagnostic weight.

IV10-02.note: Labeled medium; DEFT is easy at Upper Level. The three distractors are all generically positive dispositions and none touches competence, so a student who has only a warm/cold sense of the word still lands the key. The explanation's axis (how well vs how long vs whether vs afterward) is accurate but describes a gap the options do not really contest.

IV10-03.note: Labeled medium; reads easy. 'forgetful' has some pull via a vague low-energy/foggy association, the other two none. anxious is a clean directional opposite, which is the right kind of wrong but too far away to catch anyone.

IV10-04.note: 'recent' is a genuine trap and the best distractor in the synonym half: RUDIMENTARY means first-stage, and a student who reaches 'early' can slide from early to recent. Wrong because rudimentary indexes development, not date. costly/formal are inert.

IV10-05.note: 'escort' earns its place: a goad is the stick used to drive livestock along, so a student reasoning from the noun toward 'move someone forward' can get to escort. It is wrong because the noun's force is pressure, not accompaniment. praise/imitate are filler.

IV10-06.note: 'evasive' is the working distractor - same relational field (a way of treating someone badly) but the wrong failure: dodging rather than affronting. Some students will resist 'rude' as too plain for a hard-looking word, which is a real and legitimate pressure. Key is unambiguous.

IV10-07.note: Labeled hard; QUANDARY is common enough on Upper Level to be medium. rumor/bargain/delay are three unrelated nouns; the explanation's claim that all four 'name a situation' is true but too loose to make any of them attractive. Weakest distractor set among the hard-labeled synonyms.

IV10-08.note: 'slow to anger' is a real catch: RESILIENT is colloquially used for emotional toughness, and a student running on connotation rather than definition can read toughness as an even temper. The phrase-length options are uniform, so no length tell.

IV10-09.note: Correctly hard. The distractor logic is good: RIFE almost always collocates with something bad, so a student who has the connotation but not the meaning is steered to 'costly' or away from 'harmless'. Wrong for a reason a student actually holds - the negative charge is a feature of the contexts, not the word.

IV10-10.note: The four options are parallel by construction (want of money / company / strength / clarity), which is the correct shape: the distractors are near-misses on the same template, so the item tests which deprivation, not whether the word is negative. Best-built of the hard synonyms.

IV10-11.note: 'idle' is the reasoned trap - churl means peasant/low fellow, and a student who half-knows the etymology can reach for the lazy-lout sense. Wrong because churlish encodes ill temper toward others, not indolence. Genuinely hard on both sides: SURLY is itself Upper-Level vocabulary, so a student can know CHURLISH and still hesitate.

IV10-12.note: 'postpone' is the classic same-axis reversal and the right distractor for a pace word - it catches the student who has located the dimension but not the direction. record/approve are procedural filler drawn from the same office register as EXPEDITE, which is a reasonable secondary pull.

IV10-13.note: The strongest synonym item in the batch. All four are roles in a dispute, so the option set is a closed cast and the student must know which role arbitrates rather than merely that the word belongs to conflict. 'witness' in particular catches anyone who reads ARBITER as a neutral bystander. Labeled hard; the distractor design makes it medium because the elimination is doable from role logic.

IV10-14.note: 'rarely seen' is a directional inversion of the obviousness the word carries and will catch students who half-remember PALPABLE as something faint or ghostly. Note a slight looseness in the key: PALPABLE in ordinary use means plainly perceptible, and 'easily felt' renders the literal-touch sense; the two align here and no other option competes, so it holds.

IV10-15.note: 'tangled' is the one worth watching - matted fur is a real consequence of a wet dog and a student may reach for it. It does not survive 'completely', which fits saturation and not matting, and the sentence supplies water rather than the brambles or neglect tangling needs. Key is not contestable; the distractor is doing honest work.

IV10-16.note: The most nearly contestable of the easy items and I considered a false vote. Defense for 'scorched': the ferns are on a WINDOWSILL, which supplies sun, and scorched leaf margins are a real symptom of an unwatered plant in light. It fails because the sentence gives no season, heat or direct sun, and the causal chain it builds is a missed watering over days, which produces droop and not burn; ferns are also shade plants, so a sill is not read as a sun trap. The explanation's line - scorched 'would need direct sun rather than a missed watering' - is correct but does not acknowledge that the stem does put the plants at a window. Not a defect, but it is the sharpest distractor in the batch and it depends on a word the rationale skips past.

IV10-17.note: The post-colon list is a clean definition of the blank and rules the other three out individually, which is the right construction for an easy item. All four options are real things a coach devotes practice to, so the option set alone decides nothing - this is one of the items that should have punished the options-only solvers.

IV10-18.note: Key is solid - the stem is entirely about duration (each spring, not two years running) and only one option is a duration word. But that is also the defect: profitable/costly/confusing do not compete on the axis the stem names, so the item is answerable by picking the only temporal option without reading the rule. The thinnest sentence completion here, and the one place the batch's own authoring principle (make the options differ on some axis OTHER than the one the stem names) is violated.

IV10-19.note: Good set: all four are ways a posted timetable can fail to be trusted, so the student must use 'had not been changed since the route moved' rather than the general shape of the complaint. 'provisional' is the best of them - it also explains riders checking phones - and is defeated only by the fact that the sign was once correct.

IV10-20.note: 'impatient' is a strong, properly motivated wrong answer: a man answering the same four questions all day is the standard setup for irritation, and the student has to notice that the stem reports no feeling at all, only a lapse of attention. 'though still accurate' is the disambiguator and it is doing real work. Well made.

IV10-21.note: 'not an accident but a -------' eliminates misunderstanding and coincidence by direct contradiction, leaving precaution as the real competitor - and precaution is the attractive singleton the batch is built around. It fails on content: a propped fire door is the hazard safety rules exist to prevent, so it cannot be a precaution. Exactly the shape described in the brief - the odd option out is the distractor - and the key still wins on evidence (six visits, same wedge = habit).

IV10-22.note: 'narrow but -------' demands a term that concedes the narrowness and supplies compensating strength; only deep does. 'local' is well chosen because it is the word the shop's specialization suggests and the four-hour drive refutes - a student skimming for 'small independent business' will take it. Slight caution: narrow/deep is an idiomatic pair a coached student recognizes as a unit, which lowers the difficulty.

IV10-23.note: Labeled hard; the 'Although' makes the first blank mechanical and the second follows, so it is medium. 'difficult . . . plan' is the intended trap and it is a fair one - a student who ignores the contrast connective finds difficult perfectly sensible. Worth noting the second blanks alone (abandon/extend/describe/plan) very nearly decide it, since only 'abandon' is a response to an impassable route; that is a small options-side leak, mitigated because a blind solver must still guess which blank pairs with it.

IV10-24.note: Best two-blank item here. All four pairs are internally contrastive, so the 'yet' gives nothing away and the colon clause must be read: chapters in any order = structural break, plain declarative sentences = ordinary language. austere/lavish and impersonal/intimate are drawn from the adjacent register a student expects in literary criticism, which is why they attract. Correctly hard.

IV10-25.note: Requires actual inference - new totals higher, weather unchanged, therefore the old instrument read low - and only one option is a claim about the figures' magnitude in a fixed direction. 'rounded' is the strong distractor and I tested it as a second key: it fails because rounding is symmetric and would not produce a consistent thirty-year shortfall, and nothing in the stem says rounded down. Correctly hard.

IV10-26.note: 'habitual' is the nearest miss and I weighed it seriously: modesty sustained across a whole hour does read as practiced. It loses to 'on reflection', which signals a revision of judgment rather than a description of consistency, and to the content of the anecdote - converting an admission of failure into a credit is a designed move, not an unthinking one. 'sincere' is the reading the reflection overturns, which is the right thing for a distractor to be. Strong item.

IV10-27.note: Labeled medium; I would call it hard, because the key is a personification of a number ('a flattering figure') that a strong reader accepts easily and a weaker one will not recognize as idiomatic. The logic is sound and one-directional: warmer trial plots make sixty days optimistic, so the figure promises more than it will deliver. 'cautious' is the correct reversal-trap and 'exact' catches the student who reads only the first clause. No second defensible answer.

IV10-28.note: 'in words' is the constraint and the trailing clause supplies the contrast (they knew it by ear but could not articulate it), which defeats recall and doubt cleanly. 'perform' is the weakest of the three - it is ruled out twice over, by 'in words' and by the fact that the workshop obviously could perform the test - so the effective field is three options, not four.

IV10-29.note: Every detail in the stem points one way (Friday four o'clock, August, no summary, no questions) and the student must infer burial rather than any reception outcome. misquoted and contested are strong because they are what a student expects a committee to fear, and both require the engagement the release is engineered to prevent. Correctly hard; my pick of the batch.

IV10-30.note: DEFENSE FOR 'luck', which I think a careful student can write and which is why this is the batch's one exclusivity failure. The stem says the shop 'HAPPENS TO sit on the one corner where three bus lines meet'. 'Happens to' is the standard English marker of fortuity, and the sentence further stresses that the bakery has never once advertised - it did nothing to earn the traffic. On that reading the owner is disclaiming credit, and the since-clause explains the luck exactly as well as it explains the location: the lucky fact IS the corner. 'Puts this down entirely to luck, since the shop happens to sit on the one corner where three bus lines meet' is a fully coherent sentence and arguably the more natural one, because a person who attributes success to his address does not usually say his shop 'happens' to be there. The intended key is still better on the word 'entirely' plus the specificity of the since-clause, which names a place rather than a chance. The fix is one word in the stem: replace 'happens to sit' with 'sits' or 'stands', and 'luck' loses its footing immediately. As written, two options are defensible. Note also that 'location' is arguably too easy an anchor for a closing item.
